body: Third in the queue at the lights by the retail park, eight minutes to eight, and she has not said a word since the estate. She is sixteen, she has her bag on her knees and one shoe off. He is thinking about the fuel gauge. Then she reaches over and turns the radio down, which is the only warning he gets, and asks whether he and her mother were happy when they got married, or whether that is a stupid thing to ask. The lights change. He has the length of the bypass to answer, and he tells her the true version rather than the tidy one, largely because he is watching a lorry.
The question had been sitting in her lap since the estate, waiting for a stretch of road long enough to survive it. Turning the radio down was not a preliminary. It was the request.

Every parent of a teenager works this out eventually, and almost always by accident. The conversations that matter do not happen when you sit down opposite them and announce that you would like to talk. They happen in the car.

The reasons are close to mechanical, and they can be copied. You are side by side rather than face to face, so nothing has to be held in eye contact. There is a fixed end point, so nobody is trapped; whatever is said, it is over at the school gates. There is a legitimate reason to be in the car that is not the conversation, so the conversation can be abandoned without either party having failed at anything. And there is something else to look at, which is what most people need in order to get a hard sentence out.

None of that requires a car specifically. It requires side by side, a known ending and a reason to be there — a walk to the shop qualifies, and so does a job done together. The car is simply the version most households already own, and it comes with a radio and 46 frequencies running day and night on this dial alone.

Using it properly costs a parent something they will miss. The commute is the one hour of the day that belongs to nobody else — the podcast, the phone call, the twenty minutes of thinking the rest of the day has no room for. Handing that over is a real loss and it should be counted rather than glossed. The second cost is easier to get wrong: convert the journey into a slot for a talk and it stops working, because it becomes an occasion, and occasions get attended rather than entered. A child will tell you things at forty miles an hour that they would never say across a table, and they will stop the week you make it clear that this is why you are driving.

The journey has been quietly colonised. Four people can now travel in one car in four separate rooms — earbuds in, screens down, each of them somewhere else, and the parent is often the worst of it with a phone on the cradle and a call on speaker. Nobody decided this. It is what happens when every minute becomes a minute that could be used, and the last unbookable stretch of a family week fills up with things that were individually reasonable. What is lost is not conversation exactly. It is the shared blank space in which a conversation can start without being started.

Notice how much of the teaching in the Gospels happens on a road. Not seated in a room arranged for the purpose — walking, going somewhere else, with the lesson attached to whatever came up on the way. The Emmaus conversation is a seven-mile walk, and the reason it lands is that the journey gave it the length. Discipleship is a following word before it is a teaching word, and following happens at a pace, alongside, facing the same direction. A road teaches the skill that a classroom cannot: saying the true thing within the distance available.
So the twenty minutes are not preparation for the discipleship. They are the discipleship.

The arranged conversation deserves its due, and so does the youth group, the retreat and the weekend away. They are staffed by people who know more than most parents, and a good one will teach a child a shape they could not have got at home. But they share the same structural property: they are scheduled, and therefore attended, and a young person who has agreed to attend a thing arrives holding the version of themselves that is suitable for attending things. You will get a real conversation. What you will not reliably get is the question that had been sitting in a lap since the estate.
The thing that mattered attached itself to the journey. It could not have been booked.

A woman collects her daughter from the end of a shift at twenty to eleven on a Saturday. She gets in wearing the fleece she is not supposed to wear outside, smelling of the bakery ovens. She has ten minutes of complaint about a supervisor called Dean, and her mother makes the right noises while turning out onto the ring road. Somewhere near the second roundabout the complaining stops. Then the girl asks, at the windscreen, whether her mother actually believes all of it or whether it is just a thing she does now because she has always done it. Her mother, who has wanted this conversation for four years, gets about a mile and a half of it before they are home. The girl says thanks for the lift. Neither of them mentions it again for three months.
Nothing in that was arranged. It required a journey that existed for another reason, a stretch of road long enough to hold a hard question, and a mother with nowhere to look but forward.

The honest part is that most journeys are nothing at all. You will drive nineteen times in a row and get the weather, a grunt and a query about money. You cannot cause the twentieth, and every attempt to cause it makes it less likely — the conversational opener from a parent who has clearly been saving one up is detectable from the end of the road. Worse, when the question does arrive it will arrive when you are late, low on fuel and least equipped, and you will answer it badly at least half the time.

The nineteen empty journeys are not a failure rate. They are the rent. A young person will only put a real question into a space they are confident is not being monitored, and the only proof they will accept is a long run of journeys in which nothing was asked of them and the silence was allowed to be silent. You are not maintaining a channel of communication. You are maintaining an ordinary drive, and the ordinariness is the whole of the maintenance.

Which is why what goes on the radio for those twenty minutes is not background. It sets the temperature of the car and provides the thing that gets remarked on — and quite often it is what starts the sentence. A song can raise a subject that neither of you would have raised, and it can be discussed at arm’s length, as a song, which is exactly the distance a fifteen-year-old requires before they will say what they actually think about it.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The band runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 frequencies, 46 on air now. Most of it is music — praise and worship, gospel, country, hymns, rap, ambient and more. Some carries teaching and prayer, and some is built for children. 40 of the frequencies are international, hosted in 29 languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards. For a car with a teenager in it, though, the criteria narrow sharply: it has to be something they will not immediately switch off, and it has to have enough in it to be worth a remark.

Try HM 315.20 — Corner Cipher. It is Christian rap out of Atlanta, Marcus Reed on the mic, trap and lyrical and soul-gospel, and it talks about the block he actually came from rather than one he read about. Rap is the form that is almost entirely words, so there is always something in the car to answer. It is specific about where a person came from and what it cost, which is the register a teenager trusts. And it will not be every parent’s first choice, which is not a drawback — the currency in that car is the passenger leaving it on. A station your child does not reach over to turn down has already done more than one you enjoy more.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card — open kJubilee.com on the phone that is in the cradle and press play. It is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. You can add the page to a home screen if you want it nearer. Do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are really reaching for at which hours — which is how the next station gets built.

So do not announce anything tomorrow morning. Do not raise a subject, and do not use the journey. Put HM 315.20 on before they get in, drive the way you always drive, and let it play. Some mornings it will be nothing but the weather and Dean and the fuel gauge. Then one Tuesday a hand will come across and turn the volume down, and you will have about the length of a bypass to say the true thing rather than the tidy one.
